description:
I’ve spent 30 years leading high-performing teams in hospitality and tech, where the job was spotting early signals and getting people to act on them before a small problem became a big one.

I bring customer experience, behaviour change and product thinking, and I build with AI tools. I’m not a developer or a healthcare specialist.
summary:
Peak is a private dashboard that shows an astronaut their own health trajectory against their personal peak band, the range where they perform at their best. The band starts from a personal baseline set before the mission and adjusts in flight as mission phase and conditions change. We built a clickable prototype.

Peak addresses three gaps:

Impairment hides itself. People short on sleep rate themselves as fine while their performance declines. Peak shows the decline before the astronaut feels it.

Fear delays reporting. Reporting a problem can cost an astronaut control over their own health decisions and their seat on the mission.  In Peak, data inside the band stays private. The health team is notified only when a metric projects below the band and does not recover, on terms agreed before the mission.

Current data shows only past and present. Peak projects forward: if nothing changes, this is where the trend lands in the coming days. Each new reading updates the trajectory and recalculates the projection.

Astronauts see the decline early, act while they still control the outcome, and stay at their best for longer.
details:
What it does
Peak shows an astronaut their own health trajectory against their personal peak band, so they act early and stay at their best for longer. Each band is set from the astronaut’s pre-mission baseline. Its floor is the reference minimum for that signal. Inside the band, an expected-decline line marks the pace that is normal on a long mission.

Peak adds no new tests and no manual entry. It is designed to read the data astronauts already generate from wearables, exercise hardware and scheduled in-flight tests, and to take in new sources as they come online.

Each signal page shows the astronaut’s readings up to today, then two projections. “If nothing changes” continues the current pace. “If you act” follows the expected outcome. 

Status follows the band:

  • At peak: on or better the expected line.
  • Drifting: below the expected line but above the floor. Peak suggests a small action inside the astronaut’s existing plan, such as “Protect your sleep window tonight,” with how-to steps for workouts and tests.
  • Outside your band: below the floor. The NASA health team is notified.

While a signal is inside the band, its data stays private to the astronaut.

The Today screen stays quiet and shows only the signals that need attention. All signals covers muscle, bone health, cognition, body mass, heart rate and radiation dose.  Radiation shows cumulative dose against the 600 mSv career limit and is tracked by mission control. An illustrative solar event marker explains a dip in cognition. A History page keeps private nudges separate from NASA notifications.

Benefits and intended impact
Astronauts train to perform at their peak. On a long mission they drift from it slowly, and most won’t notice or say so until it becomes a problem. 

Peak makes the drift visible early, shows what small changes do to the line, and leaves the astronaut in control while the trend stays inside the band. That matters more on missions where help from Earth is further away.

We would measure impact by earlier reporting, fewer days from drift to action, and fewer astronauts moving outside their band. The same pattern fits firefighters, nurses and doctors, remote camp workers and pro athletes.

Tools

  • Lovable
  • Claude for research, product logic and Lovable prompts
  • Gamma and Google Slides for the deck

What makes it creative
Most health monitoring asks where your health is now and compares you to a population range. Peak asks where each astronaut’s health is heading, measured against their own best, and shows two possible futures side by side. It treats astronauts like elite athletes driven to stay at their peak, so it has no badges or scoreboards. Privacy also becomes a reason to act early: correct course inside the band and the data stays yours.

Factors we considered

  • Crew time: Peak uses measurements already on the schedule.
  • Under-reporting driven by fear of losing flight status.
  • Decline people can’t perceive in themselves.
  • False alerts: a fixed heart rate range would flag normal effort during a spacewalk, so Peak reads activity context and waits for a sustained change.
  • Alert fatigue: the Today screen shows only what needs attention.
  • Privacy and agency, balanced against crew safety.
  • Intermittent data from wearables and tests that run on uneven schedules.
  • Scope: Peak supports decisions and does not diagnose. The prototype runs on simulated data, and its floors and solar event are illustrative.
  • Validation: test with an analog mission crew, such as HERA or CHAPEA, comparing crews with and without Peak.
